series: The Light has come into the world
subtitle: Advent and Christmas: from the promises of Eden to the city full of light

days.title: The first promise
days.reflection: Right after the fall, even before announcing the consequences of sin, God makes a promise: from the offspring of the woman would come someone who would crush the serpent's head. Advent begins here, with the first announcement of the gospel, whispered in a lost garden.
story: Theology calls Genesis 3:15 the protoevangelium, the first gospel. In the middle of judgment, God is already speaking of victory.
The promise has the tone of battle. There will be enmity between the serpent and the woman, between her offspring and his. Human history comes to be read as that long conflict.
The detail is decisive: the serpent would strike the heel, but the offspring would crush the head. There would be suffering, but the mortal wound would belong to the enemy.
Throughout the Bible, every important birth rekindles that hope. Is this the promised offspring? Only in Bethlehem does the question find its answer.
days.close: Irenaeus of Lyon saw in Christ the new Adam, who retraces the path the first one undid. Advent teaches us to wait as the ancients waited: without seeing everything, but knowing that God does not forget what he promises. The Bible's first word of hope was spoken to people who had just failed.
days.application: Start a small Advent tradition today: light a candle or set aside a moment in the evening to read the day's promise and pray for those who are still waiting.

days.title: In you all will be blessed
days.reflection: God calls Abram and promises to make him a great nation, but the goal reaches beyond one family: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” The Christmas promise always had the whole world on the horizon.
story: After Babel, humanity was scattered and confused. Genesis 12 begins a new divine strategy: to bless the world through one family.
Abram was old, childless and lived in a pagan city. Humanly speaking, he was the least likely choice.
The word “blessing” appears five times in just a few verses. It is as if God were answering the five earlier curses of Genesis with a torrent of blessings.
Paul will tell the Galatians that this promise is the gospel preached beforehand: in Christ, Abraham's offspring, the blessing reaches the Gentiles.
days.close: Lesslie Newbigin reminded us that God chooses some not for privilege but for mission. Israel was chosen to be a channel, not a reservoir. The Christmas gift was not wrapped for a few; from the start it bore the name of every family on earth.
days.application: Today, pray for a nation or people who do not yet know the gospel. Try to learn a little about them.

days.title: A star out of Jacob
days.reflection: Balaam was hired to curse Israel but ended up prophesying blessing: “a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel.” God uses even unlikely mouths to announce the King who was to come.
story: Balak, king of Moab, feared Israel and paid the diviner Balaam to curse the people camped nearby.
Three times Balaam tries, and three times he can only bless. The story even has a talking donkey, showing who really governs events.
In his last prophecy, Balaam looks into a distant future: “I see him, but not now.” Star and scepter were images of royalty.
Centuries later, wise men from the East, perhaps heirs of that tradition, follow a star to Bethlehem to worship the King of the Jews.
days.close: Revelation calls Jesus “the bright morning star,” the one that appears when the night is darkest, announcing that the day is coming. Advent is living in that interval: it is still night, but the star has already been seen.
days.application: Tonight, if you can, look at the sky for a few minutes and pray, giving thanks that Christ is the light that announces the end of the night.

days.title: A throne forever
days.reflection: David wanted to build a house for God, but God answers that he himself would build a house for David: a dynasty whose throne would be established forever. No human king could fulfill that, only the Son of David who is also the Son of God.
story: David is finally at peace, living in a palace of cedar, and he is troubled that the ark of God is still in a tent.
The prophet Nathan brings a surprising answer: it is not David who will do something great for God; it is God who will do something great for David.
The promise includes a descendant who would build God's house and an everlasting kingdom. Solomon fulfilled it in part, but the kingdom divided and fell.
When the angel speaks to Mary, he takes up these words: “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and of his kingdom there will be no end.”
days.close: Every great political tradition dreams of a just and lasting ruler, and all of history shows how that dream is frustrated. Christian hope is not naive about human power; it points to a King who rules by serving and whose kingdom depends on neither elections nor armies.
days.application: Pray for the authorities of your country and city, and hand over to Christ, the eternal King, a worry about the future.

days.title: Immanuel
days.reflection: In a moment of political crisis, God offers a sign: a young woman would conceive and bear a son called Immanuel, “God with us.” The name sums up all of Christmas: God did not stay far from our fears.
story: King Ahaz was terrified. Two neighboring kingdoms had joined forces to attack Jerusalem, and the people's hearts shook “as the trees of the forest shake before the wind.”
Isaiah invites the king to ask for a sign, but Ahaz, already set on seeking help from Assyria, refuses with false piety.
God gives the sign anyway: the birth of a boy named Immanuel. Before he grew up, the threat would pass.
Matthew reads the prophecy in the light of Jesus' virgin birth. The sign given to a frightened king is fully fulfilled in the manger.
days.close: Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote from prison at Christmas that God is not ashamed of human lowliness and enters exactly where people least expect him. “God with us” does not mean problems disappear; it means we will never face them alone.
days.application: Think of a situation that has been making you afraid. Write the name “Immanuel” on a piece of paper and leave it near the place where you usually worry.

days.title: A great light
days.reflection: Isaiah speaks of a people who walked in darkness and saw a great light. The most humiliated region of Israel, Galilee, would be the first to see the dawn. God begins at the margins.
story: Galilee was the first region of Israel invaded by Assyria. It became known as “Galilee of the nations,” a mixed and despised land.
Isaiah promises that precisely there the darkness would be broken. The language is that of harvest joy and liberation from oppressors.
Matthew shows the fulfillment: Jesus begins his ministry in Galilee, in Capernaum, by the sea.
The light does not reach the center of religious power, Jerusalem, first, but the edges. That is the pattern of the gospel.
days.close: Augustine said that we have no light of our own: we are illuminated. Faith is not born from straining to see in the dark, but from the arrival of a light we did not make. Perhaps the darkest region of your life is exactly where God wants to begin.
days.application: Bring light to someone going through a dark time: a message, a visit or a prayer prayed together.

days.title: To us a child is born
days.reflection: Isaiah announces a child who bears names impossible for an ordinary baby: Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. The government will be upon his shoulders, not ours.
story: The verse continues the prophecy of light in Galilee. Liberation would come through a birth.
The four names form pairs: wisdom and power, eternity and peace. It is a description of a king like no other.
“Mighty God” is the same title used for the Lord himself in the next chapter. The promised child is not just a good king; he is God present.
Handel turned these words into one of the best-known choruses of Messiah. For centuries, the world has sung this verse at Christmas.
days.close: Bearing the government on one's shoulders is an image of responsibility. We often live as if the whole world rested on ours. Christmas puts the weight back where it belongs: on the Child who is also Mighty God.
days.application: Choose the one of the four names you need most today and pray using that name throughout the day.

days.title: The shoot of Jesse
days.theme: the Messiah full of the Spirit
days.reflection: David's dynasty would be cut down like a tree. But from the stump would come a shoot, and the Spirit of the Lord would rest upon him. God brings life out of what looked like nothing but a dead trunk.
story: In the previous chapter, Isaiah describes judgment as a forest cut down. Assyria would fall, but Judah would suffer too.
The text speaks of Jesse, David's father, rather than David. It is like going back to the family's humble origins, before the glory of the palace.
Upon the shoot would rest the Spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge and the fear of the Lord.
At Jesus' baptism, the Spirit descends on him like a dove. The promised shoot was standing before John the Baptist.
days.close: Christian tradition calls this the “Tree of Jesse,” a theme of medieval stained glass. Biblical hope is not born of human vigor but of God's faithfulness over what seemed finished. No stump is too dry for the Spirit of God.
days.application: Identify something in your life that seems to have died: a dream, a friendship, a ministry. Give it to God, asking that, if it is his will, he would make it sprout again.

days.title: Comfort my people
days.reflection: After years of judgment, God sends word to speak tenderly to Jerusalem: the time of pain is over, the guilt has been pardoned. A voice cries in the wilderness, preparing the way of the Lord.
story: Isaiah 40 opens the second great part of the book. The tone shifts from judgment to comfort.
The expression “speak tenderly” is literally “speak to the heart,” the language of someone courting a beloved. God wants to win his people back.
The voice in the wilderness calls for a work of engineering: fill in valleys, lower mountains, straighten roads. God is coming back, and the way must be ready.
All four gospels apply this text to John the Baptist. He is the voice that prepares the way for Jesus.
days.close: Preparing the way of the Lord, in Advent, means looking at the valleys of discouragement and the mountains of pride within us. God's comfort is not a pat on the back; it is real forgiveness and a presence that arrives.
days.application: Do a small piece of “road work” today: remove something that has been getting in the way of your prayer life, such as a habit, a schedule or a distraction.

days.title: Like a shepherd
days.reflection: The same Lord who comes with power is described, immediately afterward, as a shepherd who tends his flock, carries the lambs in his arms and gently leads those that are with young. In God, strength and tenderness do not contradict each other.
story: The text announces: “Behold your God!” He comes with a mighty arm, ruling and bringing his reward.
Suddenly the image changes. The arm that rules is the same one that holds lambs close to his heart.
The ewes that were nursing needed special care, because they couldn't keep up with the flock. God adjusts his pace to the weakest.
Jesus was born among shepherds and presented himself as the Good Shepherd. The prophecy gained a human face.
days.close: Many picture God only as a distant judge or as a friend without authority. Isaiah unites the two: he is powerful enough to save and tender enough to carry. Advent invites us to let ourselves be carried.
days.application: Think of someone who is fragile at the end of this year and adjust your pace to theirs: offer practical, unhurried help.

days.title: By his wounds
days.reflection: Christmas has a cross on the horizon. Isaiah's Servant bore our griefs and was pierced for our transgressions. The child in the manger was born to die in our place.
story: Isaiah introduces a mysterious figure, the Servant of the Lord, in four songs. The last one is the most surprising.
The Servant is despised, with no beauty to draw our eyes. People thought he was suffering for his own guilt.
The turning point is in the pronouns: “he was wounded for our transgressions.” His suffering was substitution.
In the book of Acts, Philip explains this text to an Ethiopian official and proclaims Jesus. The Servant has a name.
days.close: An old Christian image says that the cradle and the cross are made of the same wood. We cannot understand Christmas without Good Friday. The tenderness of the nativity is the first step of a love that would go all the way to the end.
days.application: Read all of Isaiah 53 slowly and give thanks, verse by verse, for what Christ endured for you.

days.title: The Lord Is Our Righteousness
days.reflection: Jeremiah denounces Israel's bad shepherds and promises a righteous Branch from David's line. His name will be “The Lord Is Our Righteousness.” What we could never be, God gives us in Christ.
story: Jeremiah prophesied in the last days of Judah. The kings were unjust and the people were heading into exile.
The last king, Zedekiah, had a name meaning “the Lord is my righteousness,” but he lived the opposite.
God promises a different king, who will execute justice and righteousness in the land. His name reverses the irony of the failed king.
The Reformation found here a summary of the gospel: we have no righteousness of our own, but we receive the righteousness of Christ.
days.close: Luther called this “alien righteousness”: a righteousness that comes from outside, like a garment that covers us. Christmas is God sending righteousness in person, because we would never reach it on our own.
days.application: In prayer, name an area where you try to justify yourself before others. Hand it over to Christ, your righteousness.

days.title: But you, Bethlehem
days.reflection: Micah points to Bethlehem, too little to be among the clans of Judah, as the place from which Israel's ruler would come. His origin, however, is “from of old, from ancient days.”
story: Bethlehem was a farming village about eight kilometers from Jerusalem. Its name means “house of bread.”
It was there that Ruth met Boaz and that David tended sheep. A small town with a big story.
Micah contrasts the smallness of the place with the greatness of the king's origin: he comes from eternity.
When the wise men ask where the King would be born, the scribes quote exactly this text. They knew the answer but didn't go there.
days.close: It is possible to know the prophecy and not move. The scribes had the correct information; the wise men had the willingness to walk. God keeps choosing small places and small people, and the bread of life was born in the house of bread.
days.application: Today, do something concrete with what you already know from the Word, instead of only knowing more.

days.title: The messenger
days.reflection: Malachi, the last prophet of the Old Testament, announces that God would send his messenger to prepare the way, and then the Lord himself would come to his temple. After that, four hundred years of silence.
story: The people had returned from exile, but their faith had grown cold. Blemished offerings, broken marriages and the weary question: “Where is the God of justice?”
God answers that he would come, and suddenly. But first he would send a messenger.
The Lord's coming would be like a refiner's fire and a launderer's soap: it would purify, not merely comfort.
Jesus identifies John the Baptist as that messenger. The silence of four centuries was broken by a voice in the wilderness.
days.close: The years between Malachi and Matthew look empty, but God was preparing the fullness of time. God's silence is not absence. Sometimes it is the pause before the most important word.
days.application: Set aside ten minutes of silence today, without music or screens, simply waiting on God.

days.title: The sun of righteousness
days.reflection: For those who fear the Lord's name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings. And they will go out leaping like calves released from the stall. Biblical hope ends in joy.
story: The Old Testament, in the Christian order, ends with Malachi 4. There is judgment for the arrogant, but there is light for those who fear God.
The sun's “wings” is an image of rays spreading out at dawn, reaching everything.
The scene of calves leaping as they leave the stall is full of freedom and life.
Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, echoes this image when he speaks of “the sunrise from on high” that would visit us.
days.close: Charles Wesley used this image in the Christmas hymn “Hark! the Herald Angels Sing”: Christ, the Sun of righteousness, brings light and life, risen with healing in his wings. The Christian faith is not just comfort to endure; it is healing and joy that set us on our feet.
days.application: Ask God where you need healing this year and allow yourself a moment of simple joy today, like someone set free.

days.title: Zechariah's silence
days.reflection: Zechariah and Elizabeth were old and childless. In the temple, an angel announces that their prayer has been heard: John would be born, and he would prepare the people for the Lord. Zechariah doubted and was left unable to speak until it was fulfilled.
story: Zechariah was a priest and, chosen by lot, entered the temple to burn incense, perhaps only once in his lifetime.
There the angel Gabriel appears beside the altar. His first word is “do not be afraid,” and the second, “your prayer has been heard.”
Zechariah asks for a sign, and the sign is silence. He, who should have blessed the people on coming out, cannot speak.
Nine months later, when he confirms the name John, his tongue is loosed, and the first thing he does is praise God.
days.close: Perhaps Zechariah had already stopped asking for that son. God keeps prayers that we ourselves have forgotten. The silence he lived through was not only discipline; it was also a school: whoever speaks again after waiting speaks with more praise.
days.application: Remember an old prayer you stopped praying. Bring it before God again today, with renewed confidence.

days.title: Do not be afraid, Mary
days.reflection: Gabriel visits a young woman in Nazareth and announces that she will conceive the Son of the Most High. Mary has found favor with God, not by merit but by divine choice.
story: Nazareth was an insignificant village. Nathanael would later ask whether anything good could come from there.
Mary was betrothed to Joseph. News of a pregnancy before the wedding would put her reputation, and even her life, at risk.
The angel announces a son named Jesus, who would receive David's throne and reign forever. The ancient promises converge in a womb.
Mary asks how this could be. The answer is the power of the Holy Spirit: nothing is impossible for God.
days.close: The word “favored one” comes from the same root as “grace.” Mary is an example not because she produces grace but because she receives it. The Reformers honored Mary precisely here: a humble believer who trusted God's word.
days.application: Read Luke 1:26-38 and write down a promise of God that seems impossible to you today. Pray, handing it to the God for whom nothing is impossible.

days.title: Behold, the servant of the Lord
days.reflection: Mary answers the announcement with a simple and courageous sentence: “Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” She doesn't understand everything, but she gives herself.
story: Mary does not receive a detailed plan. She doesn't know how Joseph will react or what the neighbors will say.
Even so, she answers with availability. The word “servant” indicates someone who belongs to her master.
Her answer contrasts with Zechariah's, who asked for proof. Mary asks a question, but she doesn't demand guarantees.
Then the angel departs. From then on, Mary will have to live by faith, without an angel at her side.
days.close: Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. Mary offered God her attention and her availability. The Christian life often fits into that one sentence: I don't understand everything, but I place myself in your hands.
days.application: Today, pray using Mary's words about a difficult decision or situation you are facing.

days.title: My soul magnifies the Lord
days.reflection: In Elizabeth's house, Mary sings. The Magnificat celebrates a God who looks on the humble estate of his servant, brings down the mighty and lifts up the lowly. Christmas is music before it is a present.
story: Mary hurries to the hill country of Judah to visit Elizabeth. When she hears Mary's greeting, Elizabeth's baby leaps in her womb.
Mary answers with a song full of echoes of the Old Testament, especially the prayer of Hannah, Samuel's mother.
The tone is revolutionary: God scatters the proud, brings down the mighty from their thrones and sends the rich away empty.
Mary speaks in the past tense, as if everything had already happened. To faith, God's promise is as certain as a fact.
days.close: The Magnificat has been sung at vespers by the church through the centuries and was even feared by authoritarian regimes. Magnifying God doesn't make him bigger; it makes our view of who he is bigger. Whoever magnifies God learns to see the lowly as he sees them.
days.application: Write your own short song of thanksgiving, with three concrete reasons from this year, and read it aloud.

days.title: Joseph, the just man
days.reflection: Joseph planned to send Mary away quietly, so as not to expose her. An angel appears to him in a dream and says: do not be afraid, what is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit, and you shall call his name Jesus. Joseph wakes up and obeys.
story: Matthew tells the Christmas story from Joseph's point of view. He is called “just,” someone faithful to the law and, at the same time, merciful.
Divorcing her quietly was a way to protect Mary from public shame. Even hurt, Joseph chooses kindness.
The angel reveals the child's origin and his name: Jesus, “the Lord saves,” because he would save his people from their sins.
Not a single word of Joseph's is recorded in the gospels. Only his actions: he wakes up, obeys, takes Mary as his wife and cares for the family.
days.close: There is a quiet holiness in Joseph. He accepts a stained reputation, an escape route and adoptive fatherhood. Faith that doesn't say much but obeys promptly also proclaims the gospel.
days.application: Today, do an act of obedience or care that no one will see or praise.

days.title: The sunrise from on high
days.reflection: Zechariah speaks again and prophesies about his son John and about the Messiah: because of the tender mercy of our God, the sunrise from on high will visit us, to give light to those who sit in darkness and to guide our feet into the way of peace.
story: Zechariah's song, called the Benedictus, begins by praising God who has visited and redeemed his people.
Then he turns to the child: John will be the prophet of the Most High and will go before the Lord.
The final image is that of a dawn that comes from above. It is not a light that rises from the earth but one that comes down from heaven.
The goal is practical: to guide our feet into the way of peace. The light is not only for contemplating; it is for walking.
days.close: December 21 is the longest night of the year in the northern hemisphere and the shortest in Brazil. Whatever the season, the text reminds us that God's light doesn't depend on the calendar: it visits those who sit in the shadow.
days.application: Think of someone who is “sitting in darkness” and invite them to a Christmas service or to an unhurried conversation.

days.title: There was no room
days.reflection: Joseph and Mary go to Bethlehem because of a Roman census. There Mary gives birth to her firstborn son and lays him in a manger, because there was no room for them. The King of the universe begins life in an animals' feeding trough.
story: Caesar Augustus decrees a census to collect taxes. Without knowing it, the emperor moves a poor family to the city of the prophecy.
The journey from Nazareth to Bethlehem was over a hundred kilometers. Mary was at the end of her pregnancy.
The word translated “inn” may refer to the guest room of a house. With no space there, the baby was laid where the animals ate.
Luke doesn't romanticize the scene. He describes swaddling cloths, a manger and the lack of room.
days.close: Paul says that Christ, though he was rich, became poor for our sake. The manger confronts our idea of greatness. Christmas asks a simple, uncomfortable question: in our schedule, our home and our heart, is there still room for him?
days.application: Make concrete room this Christmas week: an hour without commitments to be with God and with those you love.

days.title: Shepherds in the field
days.reflection: The first to hear the announcement of the birth were not kings or priests but shepherds working the night shift. The angel brings good news of great joy for all the people: a Savior has been born, who is Christ the Lord.
story: Shepherds were ordinary laborers and were often considered unreliable. Their testimony was not always accepted in court.
Even so, God chooses them as the first witnesses. The glory of the Lord shines around them in the middle of the field.
The announcement uses strong titles: Savior, Christ and Lord. These were words used for emperors, now applied to a baby.
The sign is surprising: a child wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger. God reveals himself in frailty.
days.close: The same God who presented himself as a shepherd in Isaiah makes shepherds the first heralds of his Son. You don't need to be important to receive the gospel, only to have attentive ears, even on the night shift.
days.application: Today, send a Christmas message with a word of hope to someone who works while others rest.

days.title: Glory to God in the highest
days.reflection: Suddenly a multitude of the heavenly host appears, praising God: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!” On Christmas Eve, heaven and earth sing together.
story: The word “host” is curious: the angels are an army, but they don't come to wage war. They come to announce peace.
Glory goes to God, in the highest. Peace comes to the earth, to people.
The phrase “with whom he is pleased” speaks of God's goodwill. Peace is not a human achievement; it is a gift of grace.
After the angels leave, the shepherds say to one another: “Let us go over to Bethlehem.” Heavenly praise becomes movement on earth.
days.close: Augustus' Pax Romana was imposed by the sword. The peace announced by the angels comes from God and begins in a reconciled heart. On Christmas Eve the invitation is simple: give glory to God and receive the peace that only he can give.
days.application: Before Christmas dinner, read Luke 2:1-20 aloud with your family or whoever is with you, and pray a prayer of thanksgiving together.

days.title: The Word became flesh
days.reflection: Merry Christmas! John sums up the mystery of this day: the Word who was with God and was God became flesh and dwelt among us. We have seen his glory, full of grace and truth.
story: John doesn't tell the story of the shepherds or the wise men. He looks at Christmas from eternity.
“In the beginning was the Word” echoes Genesis. The One through whom everything was created now enters creation as a child.
“Became flesh” is a strong expression. It is not a human appearance: God takes on a body, weariness, hunger and tears.
“Dwelt” means pitched his tent. As in the wilderness, God comes to live in the middle of his people's camp.
days.close: Athanasius wrote that the Son of God became man so that we might share in the life of God. C. S. Lewis called the incarnation “the grand miracle,” on which all the others depend. Today we celebrate not a memory but the certainty that God is with us forever.
days.application: Celebrate joyfully today, but set aside a moment to worship: read John 1:1-14 and tell Jesus, in your own words, what it means to you that he came.

days.title: My eyes have seen
days.reflection: In the temple, old Simeon takes the child in his arms and prays: now I can depart in peace, for my eyes have seen your salvation, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel.
story: Simeon was righteous and devout and was waiting for the consolation of Israel. The Spirit had revealed to him that he would not die before he had seen the Christ.
Forty days after the birth, Joseph and Mary bring Jesus to the temple to fulfill the law. They are a poor family, offering two turtledoves.
Simeon recognizes the Messiah in an ordinary baby, among the many others being presented that day.
He also tells Mary something hard: a sword would pierce her own soul. Salvation would come with pain.
days.close: Simeon's song, the Nunc Dimittis, has been sung for centuries in evening prayer. It teaches us that whoever has seen salvation can rest, in life and in death. After Christmas, the question is: have my eyes truly seen?
days.application: Pray Simeon's prayer before going to sleep tonight, giving thanks for the year and handing to God what remains unanswered.

days.title: Anna, the prophetess
days.reflection: Anna, an elderly widow, served God in the temple with fasting and prayer night and day. When she sees the child, she gives thanks and begins to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
story: Anna had been married only seven years and had been a widow for decades. A life that could have been marked by bitterness.
Instead, she made the temple her place. Her hope had withstood many years of silence.
Luke calls her a prophetess and names her tribe, Asher, one of the nearly forgotten northern tribes.
When she meets Jesus, Anna doesn't keep the news to herself. She becomes one of the first evangelists.
days.close: Anna's perseverance shows that waiting is not wasted time when it is lived with God. Elderly believers are a treasure for the church: they carry memory and hope. Whoever waits well recognizes the fulfillment when it comes.
days.application: Visit or call an elderly person from your church or family and ask how God has been faithful in their life.

days.title: The wise men and the star
days.reflection: The wise men come from the East following a star. When they see it stop over the house, they rejoice exceedingly with great joy, go in, fall down and worship the child, offering gold, frankincense and myrrh.
story: The wise men were students of the stars, probably from Persia or Babylon. They were foreigners of another religion.
They first come to Jerusalem, to the palace, looking for the king in the obvious place. Herod is troubled, and all the city with him.
The star leads them to Bethlehem. Matthew speaks of a house, which suggests that some time had passed since the birth.
Tradition reads the gifts as symbols: gold for the King, frankincense for God and myrrh for the one who was going to die.
days.close: T. S. Eliot wrote a poem about the journey of the magi, in which one of them concludes that this birth was also a kind of death to his old world. Truly meeting Christ changes the road home: they returned “by another way.”
days.application: Offer Jesus a concrete gift today: time, a talent or an offering for someone in need.

days.title: Flight into Egypt
days.reflection: Herod wants to kill the child. Warned in a dream, Joseph flees by night with Mary and Jesus to Egypt. The Savior of the world begins life as a refugee.
story: Herod the Great was known for his cruelty and paranoia. He had even members of his own family killed.
Joseph receives another dream and, once again, obeys immediately. He rises by night and leaves.
Egypt had large Jewish communities at that time. It was a possible refuge, out of Herod's reach.
Matthew quotes Hosea: “Out of Egypt I called my Son.” Jesus retraces Israel's story, coming out of Egypt as the people did in the exodus.
days.close: Christmas doesn't happen in a postcard world. There is violence, fear and flight. God's presence did not prevent the threat, but it guided the family through it. Jesus knows from experience the pain of those who have had to leave everything to survive.
days.application: Pray today for refugees and displaced families, and look for a concrete way to help an organization that cares for them.

days.title: In the fullness of time
days.reflection: Paul sums up Christmas in theology: when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.
story: The Galatians were going back to trusting the law to be accepted by God. Paul answers by showing what Christ has done.
“Fullness of time” suggests a divine clock. God acted at the exact moment in history.
“Born of woman” affirms Jesus' full humanity. “Born under the law” shows that he fulfilled everything we failed to fulfill.
The final goal is adoption. That is why the Spirit cries out within us: “Abba, Father.”
days.close: On the next-to-last day of the year, it is good to remember that time is in God's hands. The same Lord who waited for the fullness of time to send his Son also guides our calendar. We end the year not as employees under review, but as beloved children.
days.application: Review the year in prayer: give thanks, confess and hand your plans for next year to the Father.

days.title: A city full of light
days.theme: the hope of the new creation
days.reflection: The last day of the year ends with the Bible's last vision: a city that needs neither sun nor moon, because the glory of God gives it light and its lamp is the Lamb. The light that came into the world at Christmas will shine forever.
story: Revelation 21 describes the new Jerusalem coming down out of heaven. It is not an escape from creation but its renewal.
There will be no temple, because God himself and the Lamb will be its temple. The presence that filled the tabernacle will fill everything.
The nations will walk by the light of that city. The promise made to Abraham, of blessing for all the families of the earth, is fulfilled.
The Lamb, who was born in Bethlehem and died on the cross, is the city's lamp. The series begins and ends in Christ.
days.close: We began the month in the lost garden and we end it in the city full of light. Between the two stands the manger. Whatever darkness this year has brought, the last word of history is light. Let us cross into the new year with that hope.
days.application: Before midnight, read Revelation 21:1-7 and pray, handing the new year to God and asking to live as a child of the light.
